title: Background Rehydration Controller and Hotpatch API
content:
Summary:

This is a working draft for a Background Rehydration Controller (BRC) and a small Hotpatch API intended to make safe, low-latency weight repairs and small binary deltas to model parameters while minimizing impact to in-flight inference. The goal is to provide a pragmatic, low-risk mechanism for: applying tiny fixes to weight shards, repairing corrupted mmap pages, and gradually rehydrating evicted/lazy-loaded slices without triggering large-scale cold starts or QoS regressions.

Context and motivation:
- We operate with heavy use of lazy loading, mmap-backed weight residency, and safetensors files on object storage.
- Operational incidents show two recurring pain points: 1) single-page corruption / checksum mismatch on a shard that causes request failures, and 2) need to deliver micropatches (e.g., quantization correction, dtype fix) to a small subset of layers without reloading whole model.
- Full hot-swap (swap entire model/large shard) remains the right tool for major updates. The BRC + Hotpatch API is designed for smaller, frequent, operational fixes and background rehydration of cache-friendly slices.

Goals:
- Allow atomic application of small delta patches (≤ 5% of shard size, configurable) with bounded memory overhead.
- Perform background rehydration of evicted weight pages guided by runtime telemetry so that hot prefixes experience minimal latency impact.
- Provide safe fencing so inference jobs either use pre-patch or post-patch consistent views for the extent of a request.
- Integrate with existing mmap loader, safetensors checksum verification, and KV cache reconciliation logic.
- Expose metrics and a minimal operator API for forced repair and patch rollout.

Non-goals:
- Not intended to replace full shard hot-swap or rolling model version rollouts.
- Not a migration path for large quantization changes that require kernel recompilation.

High-level design:
1) Representation: Patch bundles
- A patch bundle contains: target-model-id, shard-id, list of (byte-range, patch-binary, checksum), metadata: reason, max-apply-duration, rollout-policy.
- Patches are expected to be small contiguous byte-range substitutions or compressed delta-encoded segments created by the model onboarding tooling.

2) BRC components (in-process with serving runtime):
- Patch Coordinator (PC): receives patch bundles via the Hotpatch API. Validates bundle checksums, ensures compatibility with committed shard fingerprint.
- Range Guardian (RG): lightweight in-memory map tracking protected byte ranges per shard (fences). Ensures in-flight requests that overlap ranges are allowed to finish against a consistent view.
- Background Rehydrator (BR): worker pool responsible for fetching and streaming missing pages into RAM/mmap and optionally applying delta patches in-place or staged. Schedules rehydration priority using a scoring heuristic (see Scheduling policy).
- Safe Committer (SC): orchestrates the final atomic switch to the patched view: commit(safetensors fingerprint update, update residency map, release fences).

3) Patch lifecycle:
- Submit -> Validate -> Stage -> Fence -> Apply -> Commit -> Reconcile
- Submit: API call uploads patch bundle or references an object store URL.
- Validate: PC checks that base fingerprint matches live shard, verifies per-range checksums. If mismatched base fingerprint, abort and require full hot-swap path.
- Stage: BR downloads patch ranges to a per-shard staging area (memory or ephemeral file).
- Fence: RG inserts a fence for each byte-range; RG increments a per-range in-flight counter if requests are currently reading overlapping pages. Requests check the RG before reading a range and either proceed (if using pre-patch snapshot) or wait for short grace.
- Apply: BR applies the binary delta into staged pages; if patch is in-place safe (size equal), it can write to an anonymous mmap segment, then atomically remap. For smaller-patch-in-large-file, we use copy-on-write to an ephemeral file followed by an mmap_remap under a write-lock.
- Commit: SC updates the shard fingerprint and updates the loader residency map; fences are then released once new readers pick up the post-patch view.

Fencing / Consistency model:
- Request view semantics: each inference request binds to a model-version-snapshot at the start. Snapshot contains list of shard fingerprints and patch generation numbers.
- When a patch fence exists for byte-range R, readers that started before the fence use snapshot N (pre-patch) and proceed; readers starting after fence completion will see snapshot N+1 (post-patch).
- To avoid long stalls, we set a configurable maximum wait timeout for new requests that would overlap active patches; after timeout the new request selects a compatible fallback model variant or is rejected per policy.

Scheduling policy for background rehydration and patch application:
- Scoring inputs: per-layer recent access frequency (prefix heatmap), request latency SLO headroom, shard residency memory pressure, patch urgency (operational priority), and worker pool load.
- Rehydration prioritizes ranges with highest access frequency and lowest resident fraction. Low-critical patches (e.g., telemetry-only) are scheduled during low load windows. Urgent patches bypass usual backoff and preempt rehydration tasks.
- Rate limiting: configurable global throttle to avoid saturating IO or GPU bandwidth. We use a token-bucket style limiter per-node and global backpressure signals from the serving runtime.

Interaction with mmap / safetensors / KV cache:
- mmap: We avoid in-place modifications of a live mmap backed by shared file; instead, we allocate a small anonymous mmap region for patched pages and update a per-shard page-mapping indirection table. The runtime page access path consults the indirection table to map logical page -> physical mmap region.
- safetensors: Patch validation requires verifying the original safetensors fingerprint; when committing, the SC produces a new safetensors-style metadata entry (not necessarily rewriting the entire file) with updated checksums. Object store metadata tracks patch generations.
- KV cache: When patches touch parameters that are cached in KV (key/value cache for KV attention or prefix cache), BR will evict conflicting KV entries and trigger a lazy recompute for next requests. We provide a small compatibility shim that identifies affected KV keys from layer->kv key mapping.

Hotpatch API (minimal):
- POST /hotpatch/submit { model_id, shard_id, patch_url_or_blob, max_apply_duration_s, priority } -> returns patch_id or error
- GET /hotpatch/status/{patch_id} -> returns state: pending|staging|fencing|applying|committing|done|failed
- POST /hotpatch/force-commit/{patch_id} (operator-only) -> attempts commit even if some noncritical fences are active
- POST /rehydration/inspect { model_id, shard_id } -> returns rough residency map (approx) and suggested ranges to prefetch (admin only)
- Webhook/Callback on completion to inform higher-level rollout controller

Metrics and observability:
- patch.apply.count, patch.apply.duration_seconds (histogram), patch.failures{reason}, rehydration.bytes_fetched, rehydration.pages_prefetched, fence.wait_seconds, live_snapshots_active, patch.memory_overhead_bytes
- Logs include patch_id, shard_id, reason, staging checksums, and operator comments. Link patches to incidents and GH PRs where possible.

Failure modes and recovery:
- Validation failure: abort and report; operator must opt into full hot-swap.
- Mid-apply node crash: SC uses commit log to reconcile on restart. Staged patches that didn't commit are garbage-collected after TTL.
- Long-lived readers prevent commit: after configurable threshold, we either force-close stale readers (operator opt-in) or roll the patch to a lower-priority window.
- Partial commit across nodes (in Dedicated mode): commit is orchestrated by central control plane that ensures all nodes reach a consistent fingerprint; nodes that fail to update rollback to previous mapping and alert.

Security and operational controls:
- Patches must be signed by a trusted key; ingestion requires operator permission or a pre-approved automation principal.
- Rate limits and size caps enforced per-tenant to avoid noisy-neighbor abuse.

Implementation notes and integration tasks (TODOs):
- Prototype indirection table for per-shard page mapping and integrate into slow-path param read. (Owner: Miguel)
- Extend safetensors metadata to allow patch-generation entries; spec and GH PR required. (Owner: Priya)
- Small API server for hotpatch submissions + auth checks. (Owner: Liam)
- Add telemetry hooks into existing KV cache eviction logic. (Owner: Ava)
- Chaos tests: simulate readers overlapping fences, node restarts mid-apply. (SRE collaboration)

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Inline patch vs staged-file approach tradeoff for performance and memory: staged-file reduces risk but increases IO. Need empirical comparison.
- How aggressive should forced eviction be when patches impact KV cache? Conservative eviction minimizes recompute cost but increases tail latency.
- Operator UX: do we offer automated rollouts with canarying patches to a subset of nodes? That would complicate snapshot bookkeeping.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: safety and per-request determinism are priorities. Feedback welcome on the fencing semantics (snapshot model) and the memory overhead budget for staging.
- Slack thread: #runtime-rehydration for discussion.

Appendix: simple patch lifecycle example:
1) Ops submits patch to fix 4KB checksum mismatch in layer 32 (patch_id p123).
2) PC validates fingerprint; BR stages the 4KB patch into memory.
3) RG sees 2 active readers touching that page; creates fence and waits with 30s timeout.
4) Once readers finish, BR applies patch to staged page, SC updates indirection table so new readers map to patched anonymous mmap.
5) Commit log is written, metrics emitted, RG releases fence, and patch_id p123 -> done.

End of draft.
